A frantic debate is unfolding over whether and how to slow down the pace of AI development to avoid some kind of cataclysm. Yet these discussions tend to skate past one important question: If the people building AI really think that their product could bring about human extinction, how exactly do they think that would work? Any number of ways, it turns out. But first, we should start with the basics. Any good answer must begin with the so-called alignment problem: the possibility that AI systems pursue goals that their creators did not intend, resulting in catastrophic harm. In the canonical thought experiment, humans instruct a superintelligent AI system to carry out the seemingly banal task of maximizing paper-clip production. The misaligned machine concludes that it should hoard all of the metal on Earth to make paper clips, and goes on to exterminate the human race to eliminate the competition for resources. keptItems.title: Trump Should Stop Hosting Summits
keptItems.summaryEvidence: State visits are a normal and necessary part of diplomacy. National leaders should, from time to time, sit with one another in person and have candid conversations. Summit meetings between the American president and his counterparts from Moscow and Beijing are particularly tricky because of the innately tense relationship between two adversaries. Food and hospitality are part of the festivities, but in the end, such summits provide important human contact at the highest level, and as a result, crucial business can get done that might not be possible over a telephone or in messages delivered through ambassadors. At least, that’s how these visits are supposed to work. In the Donald Trump White House, summits are hazardous excursions during which the interests of the United States are shoved aside by a president whose cringe-inducing admiration of dictators makes these meetings into rituals of American humiliation. The country would be better off if Trump just stopped hosting or attending them. Summits are a problem in this administration for two reasons. The most important is that Trump’s unpredictability and obvious lack of preparation make them dangerous. State visits require a lot of political groundwork, and leaders rarely go into top-level meetings without a set of issues they’ve already agreed to discuss. This agenda-setting gets done long before a president actually sits down with another head of state so that stray asides (or rising tempers) do not derail whatever business needs to be discussed. keptItems.title: Another Female Democrat Is Mean, Apparently
keptItems.summaryEvidence: In February 2024, according to a former staff member who told the story to The New York Times , Representative Mary Peltola , an Alaska Democrat running for the Senate, pushed an aide. As the Times put it in a report published yesterday, Peltola “shoved a male employee in the chest with one hand, causing him to stumble backward.” You might wonder why the paper of record is reporting this detail. Did the employee then tumble off a cliff and die? The Times does not mention any bodily harm, beyond the backward stumble. The encounter is instead offered as evidence of what the Times calls “a campaign and congressional office marked by chaos.” Chaos . The attempted exposé of Peltola is the latest installment in a familiar genre. Democratic staffers (they are almost always Democrats) complain off the record about the private behavior of their boss, who is almost always female, toward them. The behavior in question ranges from inappropriate to, more often, somewhat inappropriate to completely appropriate. One notorious example concerns former Representative Katie Porter of California, who shouted, as she was being filmed, “Get out of my fucking shot,” at a staffer. Although nobody enjoys being shouted at, there is a certain urgency about getting the staff out of a camera shot that is supposed to focus exclusively on the principal. Sports fanaticism was on the rise in America in the 1920s, when superstar athletes (ever heard of Babe Ruth?) drew crowds of tens of thousands of both sexes, across a variety of sports. Pratt Allen acknowledged herself to be “a pretty good baseball fan as women go,” eager to applaud a good play and posssessing extensive knowledge of the sport rivaling that of her male companions. manifest.title: Trump’s Public Service Announcement: ‘Love Me’

A pause. Then a dozen more Trumps. The pattern repeats several times. There are plugs for some of his priorities—such as cutting taxes and defending police officers—but one message stays on the screen for fully half of the 30-second commercial: AmericA will never be a communist country . Throughout, an R&B song plays in the background, with falsetto voices singing, over and over: “Love me … Love me … Love me …” At the end comes this: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.” Huh? If the use of taxpayer dollars seems odd—and it should—the explanation that the White House gave me is even more bizarre. I also received a list of supposedly comparable PSAs from past presidents: George W. Bush spent federal dollars urging the youth of America not to do drugs. manifest.title: Trump Should Stop Hosting Summits
manifest.summaryEvidence: State visits are a normal and necessary part of diplomacy. National leaders should, from time to time, sit with one another in person and have candid conversations. Summit meetings between the American president and his counterparts from Moscow and Beijing are particularly tricky because of the innately tense relationship between two adversaries. Food and hospitality are part of the festivities, but in the end, such summits provide important human contact at the highest level, and as a result, crucial business can get done that might not be possible over a telephone or in messages delivered through ambassadors. At least, that’s how these visits are supposed to work. In the Donald Trump White House, summits are hazardous excursions during which the interests of the United States are shoved aside by a president whose cringe-inducing admiration of dictators makes these meetings into rituals of American humiliation. The country would be better off if Trump just stopped hosting or attending them. Summits are a problem in this administration for two reasons. The most important is that Trump’s unpredictability and obvious lack of preparation make them dangerous. State visits require a lot of political groundwork, and leaders rarely go into top-level meetings without a set of issues they’ve already agreed to discuss. This agenda-setting gets done long before a president actually sits down with another head of state so that stray asides (or rising tempers) do not derail whatever business needs to be discussed. manifest.title: The Doomed Midterm Strategy Some Republicans Are Trying
manifest.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. With the midterm elections just 40 days away, Republicans are running hard—many of them away from President Trump. Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican whose district Trump won by 15 points in 2024, recently released an ad critiquing the administration’s immigration enforcement, saying that Hispanic voters feel “betrayed.” Byron Donalds, the GOP’s nominee for governor of Florida, scrubbed most references to Trump from his website—a notable move considering that the foundation of Donalds’s entire career has been fidelity to the Donald. The Senate contenders Mike Rogers of Michigan and Ashley Hinson of Iowa are both calling for an end to the Iran war. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, has even suddenly changed his mind and now believes that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. The number of prominent Republicans distancing themselves from Trump has accelerated, or at least reached a critical mass, in the past 10 days. The shift is interesting—first, as an indication of what information GOP candidates are receiving privately about the president’s unpopularity and its drag on them, and second, because public critiques of Trump from Republicans have been vanishingly rare, no matter how unwise, outrageous, or unpopular his actions have been. manifest.title: Another Female Democrat Is Mean, Apparently
manifest.summaryEvidence: In February 2024, according to a former staff member who told the story to The New York Times , Representative Mary Peltola , an Alaska Democrat running for the Senate, pushed an aide. As the Times put it in a report published yesterday, Peltola “shoved a male employee in the chest with one hand, causing him to stumble backward.” You might wonder why the paper of record is reporting this detail. Did the employee then tumble off a cliff and die? The Times does not mention any bodily harm, beyond the backward stumble. The encounter is instead offered as evidence of what the Times calls “a campaign and congressional office marked by chaos.” Chaos . The attempted exposé of Peltola is the latest installment in a familiar genre. Democratic staffers (they are almost always Democrats) complain off the record about the private behavior of their boss, who is almost always female, toward them. The behavior in question ranges from inappropriate to, more often, somewhat inappropriate to completely appropriate. One notorious example concerns former Representative Katie Porter of California, who shouted, as she was being filmed, “Get out of my fucking shot,” at a staffer. Although nobody enjoys being shouted at, there is a certain urgency about getting the staff out of a camera shot that is supposed to focus exclusively on the principal.
